space.$description: One spacing scale for both products, replacing the four independent rhythms the Stage 1 audit found in v0. The step number is the value in eighths of the base step — 100 is 8px, 200 is 16px — so a number carries a ratio rather than a position in a list, and inserting a step later does not renumber everything after it. Density differences between Market and Move are expressed by which step a component selects, never by a second scale. Every value is a multiple of 4 except space.25, which exists for hairline nudges.

0.$description: No space. A named zero, so that a component removing a gap in one density or one direction states it as a token rather than dropping out of the system.

25.$description: The smallest step. For optical corrections and gaps between elements that are meant to read as one object — an icon and its immediately adjacent glyph, a badge and its border.

50.$description: The tightest real gap. Separates parts within a single control: a label from its helper glyph, stacked lines inside one cell.

100.$description: The base step, and the unit the numbering is derived from. The default gap between related items in a group and the inner padding of small controls.

150.$description: The half step between 100 and 200. It exists because the gap between 8 and 16 is where compact layouts do most of their work, and Move needs a rung there rather than a choice between cramped and loose.

200.$description: The comfortable default: inner padding of a card or a standard control, and the gap between sibling items in a list.

250.$description: The half step between 200 and 300, for the same reason 150 exists — the comfortable range needs a rung between its default and its next size up.

300.$description: Separates one group of related things from the next within a section. The first step that reads as a division rather than a gap.

400.$description: Separates sections of a page. Large enough that a divider line becomes optional rather than necessary.

500.$description: A major break between regions of a screen, and the outer margin of a roomy layout.

600.$description: The largest step. The top of the scale is deliberately low: anything needing more room than this is a layout decision — a grid, a max width, a viewport unit — and not a spacing token.

radius.$description: Corner radii. Four values, because a radius is a soft signal and more of them produces inconsistency rather than nuance. Numbered in the same style as space — the number carries a ratio rather than a position in a list — but against its own base of 4px, so radius.200 is twice radius.100 and is not the same measurement as space.200. This sentence previously claimed the two scales shared the eighths convention and therefore read alike; they do not, radius.100 is 4px where that convention predicts 8px, and a reader who trusted it would have mis-set every corner in the system.

0.$description: Square. For anything that meets an edge or another element flush — a full-bleed image, a table cell, a sheet against the viewport.

100.$description: The small radius, for controls and other elements the hand interacts with directly: inputs, buttons, chips.

200.$description: The container radius, for things that hold other things: cards, panels, popovers, sheets.

full.$description: Fully rounded. Named rather than numbered because it is a shape instruction, not a measurement: it produces a pill or a circle at any size, which is what avatars, dots and pill badges actually want. The 9999 is an implementation detail of expressing that in px.

stroke.$description: Border and outline widths. Two values, because two is what the seven components actually draw and a third would be invented rather than found. Its own scale rather than a reach into space, because a stroke and a gap are different jobs that happen to share two numbers: styles/focus.css drew the outline width and the outline offset from space.25 on adjacent lines, one of them ink and the other emptiness, and nothing in the system could tell them apart. Numbered against its own base of 1px — the hairline — so the number is a multiple of the thinnest line the system draws, in the same style as space and radius and, like radius, on a base of its own. Every mature system consulted keeps this separate: Polaris, Primer and Spectrum each ship a stroke scale distinct from spacing rather than expressing a stroke as a spacing step, and 1px and 2px are steps on all three. They are not the whole of any of them — Polaris also carries 0, 0.66px and 4px — and this scale deliberately stops where Mizan's own evidence stops, which decision 026 argues.

100.$description: The hairline, and the width of nearly every line in the system: the edge of a control, the outline of a card, the divider between list rows. One device pixel at 1x, and deliberately not scaled by density — a hairline that thickens with the control stops reading as an edge and starts reading as a frame.

200.$description: The emphatic stroke, for a line that has to be seen rather than merely bound a shape: the focus outline, the busy indicator's ring, and the inline-start mark that flags low stock or a surge fare. Twice the hairline is the smallest step that reads as deliberate at arm's length; anything between the two is a rendering accident on a fractional-density screen.
